title: Natural-language analytics with Genie
summary: Three Genie roles, one question path, curation that keeps answers on contract, the asker's own permissions, and a benchmark with a review loop that is authored evidence until a dated run exists.
outcomes: Place Genie One, Genie Agents and Genie Code by role, and read each documentation page's own name for them.
Trace a question through interpretation, generated SQL, result and validation, and name the step that drifted.
Curate a Genie Agent with few described tables, business semantics in SQL, example SQL, specific instructions and trusted assets.
Predict answers for different askers under their own permissions, and write a benchmark with guarded classes and a review loop.
startingAssumptions: A metric contract exists for the numbers the space will answer, with grain, numerator, denominator and restatement rules.
Unity Catalog privileges (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT) are familiar from the business intelligence module's access primer; the later governance track owns the full model.

The worked figures come from this module's own five-day synthetic week of the published line-rate table, Monday to Friday, which does not overlap the business intelligence module's reconciliation sheet; its line values are not that module's.
editorialRationale: Natural-language analytics fails quietly: answers are fluent, fast and plausible. The module therefore starts by separating the three Genie roles and the names each page uses, gives every answer a five-step path so a wrong one can be placed, then treats scope, descriptions, business semantics, examples, instructions and trusted assets in the documented order before access, which is the one failure curation cannot fix. The benchmark and review loop close the module, with the authored benchmark kept apart from any claim about a live space.

claims.description: Genie is a family of Databricks natural-language experiences: Genie One for business users, Genie Agents as domain-specific environments a data team configures, and Genie Code as the AI coding and data assistant for developers.
claims.context: Databricks on AWS documentation, September 2026; names and scope change.

claims.description: Genie Agents were formerly Genie Spaces and Genie One was previously Databricks One. The older benchmark, knowledge-store, agent-mode and trusted-assets URLs now redirect to current Genie Agents pages; URL names alone do not date the behavior.
claims.context: Page titles and snippets as confirmed by search on 2026-09-23.

claims.description: A Genie Agent converts a natural-language question into SQL by selecting relevant names and descriptions from annotated tables and columns, and responds with the generated query and a results table when it can.
claims.context: Mechanism described in general terms by the documentation.

claims.description: Curation guidance: aim for five or fewer tables and few columns, prejoin related tables into views or metric views, start small and iterate on feedback; Genie uses Unity Catalog names and descriptions.
claims.context: Current best-practices page; counts and limits may change.

claims.description: The documented order of curation inputs is well-documented datasets, SQL expressions for business semantics, example SQL queries, and text instructions only as a last resort; example SQL teaches common ambiguous prompts; instructions should be specific and consistent with example SQL.

Unity Catalog metric views define a measure once, separately from the fields used to group and filter it, and can be queried from SQL, notebooks, dashboards, Genie Agents and alerts; a knowledge store holds SQL expressions for measures, filters and dimensions with synonyms.
claims.context: Unity Catalog semantics and Genie knowledge store pages; YAML syntax is versioned.

claims.description: In Chat mode, exact reuse of a parameterized SQL example produces a verified answer. Parameterized queries and attached Unity Catalog SQL functions are trusted assets; users require EXECUTE on the functions. This does not prove correct question interpretation.
claims.context: Older trusted-assets page; recheck current behaviour.

claims.description: Standalone Genie Agents apply the asker's Unity Catalog data permissions and row filters or masks; embedded author credentials supply warehouse access. Editors also need the SQL entitlement, data SELECT, warehouse CAN USE and agent CAN EDIT. Autogenerated dashboard companions follow the dashboard credential model.
claims.context: Create and manage a Genie Agent page; permission names may change.

claims.description: When Genie cannot answer, it might ask a clarification question or explain that it cannot answer from the provided information; specific clarification instructions are recommended over vague ones.

Genie benchmarks are test questions whose generated SQL and results are compared with a SQL Answer; questions without one need manual review; two to four phrasings per question are recommended; agent-mode benchmarks are graded by an LLM judge.
claims.context: Use benchmarks page; the product feature, not an authored benchmark.

claims.description: The Monitor tab exposes questions, feedback and review requests to CAN MANAGE users. Full conversations and results depend on sharing: Private conversations expose prompts to managers, not the full exchange or results.

Agent mode, formerly Research Agent, answers exploratory questions by planning, running several SQL queries and iterating, and returns a report with citations; benchmarks in agent mode are graded by an LLM judge.
claims.context: Availability and status to verify per workspace.

claims.description: Publishing with Enable Genie on, the default, creates a companion agent. Autogenerated companions inherit the dashboard credential model; linked agents retain their own settings. Companion instructions cannot be edited in the agent UI; republishing updates the companion.
claims.context: Default may change; check the publish dialog.

claims.description: Prompt matching includes entity matching, which maps user terminology to stored column values. Format-assistance samples use author permissions and become shared agent context; view-backed row filters or masks and dynamic views require author review of entity matching.
claims.context: Curation page; configuration details on the linked pages.

concepts.definition: The Databricks family of natural-language data experiences: Genie One, Genie Agents and Genie Code, sharing Unity Catalog governance.
concepts.example: A supervisor asks in Genie One, a curated Genie Agent answers, and the analyst used Genie Code to write the curation SQL.

concepts.definition: The simplified business-user interface for opening AI/BI dashboards, asking data questions in natural language and running Databricks Apps.
concepts.example: A North plant supervisor opens Genie One on a phone and asks about line 3.

concepts.definition: A domain-specific environment a data team configures with data, descriptions, examples, instructions and trusted assets, which in the standalone setup turns questions into SQL run under each asker's permissions.
concepts.example: Cinderline's North plant quality agent holds the accepted daily line-rate table and the exclusion counts.

concepts.definition: The AI coding and data assistant for developers inside notebooks, the SQL editor, the pipelines editor, dashboards and MLflow.
concepts.example: The analyst asks Genie Code to draft the parameterized example query for line rates.

concepts.definition: The step that maps a question's business words onto the space's tables, columns, measures and filters before SQL is written.
concepts.example: 'Worst line' is read as the highest ratio-of-sums defect rate per line_id.

concepts.definition: Comparing a generated answer's SQL properties and result with a contracted reference query over the same snapshot.
concepts.example: Line 2 at 6.6% fails against the reference 6.1% as wrong arithmetic.

concepts.definition: A reply that names the competing readings of an ambiguous question and asks which one the asker means, instead of guessing.
concepts.example: 'Do you mean defective units or rejected inspections?'

concepts.definition: Choosing the few tables, views and metric views an agent may read and describing them so questions land on the right data.
concepts.example: The North space keeps the accepted table and drops raw inspections and quarantine.

concepts.definition: Unity Catalog comments that say what a row is and what each column means, which Genie reads to interpret questions.
concepts.example: A comment says restated marks a day whose value was replaced.

concepts.definition: A Unity Catalog object that defines measures once, separately from the fields used to group and filter them, for SQL, dashboards and Genie.
concepts.example: unit_defect_rate defined as try_divide(SUM(defective_units), SUM(inspected_units)) by line_id and business_day.

concepts.definition: A curated question-and-query pair or SQL definition in a space that shows Genie how a common or ambiguous prompt maps to correct SQL.
concepts.example: 'Worst line over five days' paired with the SUM-over-SUM query.

concepts.definition: Plain-language guidance in a space, used last and written specifically, for rules that SQL definitions and examples cannot carry.
concepts.example: 'When a question says defects without units or inspections, ask which.'

concepts.definition: A parameterized example query or Unity Catalog SQL function in a space; a response built from one is described as a verified answer in Chat mode.
concepts.example: line_rate(line_id, business_day) answers 'line 3 yesterday' with the trusted-asset response.

concepts.definition: For a standalone agent, query data access uses the asker while author credentials supply the warehouse. Dashboard companions have a separate credential model.
concepts.example: ana-north gets no quarantine rows because she holds no SELECT on quarantine.conflicts.

concepts.definition: A test question with phrasings and expected SQL and result properties, used to judge a space's answers before and after changes.
concepts.example: 'Worst line over five days?' expects SUM over SUM per line and line 2 at 6.1%.

concepts.definition: The repeated cycle of running benchmarks, reading monitored feedback, classifying failures and making one curation change per class.
concepts.example: A wrong-arithmetic failure leads to the metric view, then a dated rerun.

concepts.definition: A question whose answer is not in the space's data or definitions, which should be refused with a reason rather than guessed.
concepts.example: 'What caused line 2's defects on day 3?' has no cause data in the space.

concepts.definition: A Genie mode that plans multi-step analyses, runs several SQL queries and returns a cited report instead of one query and result.
concepts.example: 'Why did line 2 worsen this month?' answered as a report with supporting tables.

concepts.definition: A Genie Agent created automatically from a published AI/BI dashboard's datasets when the Enable Genie toggle is on.
concepts.example: Publishing the North plant dashboard creates an agent over its three datasets.

concepts.definition: A space setting that helps Genie map the value a user types to the value stored in a column.
concepts.example: A supervisor types 'north' and the stored plant value 'North plant' is matched.

concepts.definition: Records of Genie Agent activity and feedback in the account's audit system table, attributed to the asking user.
concepts.example: A query of system.access.audit filtered to service_name 'aibiGenie' lists feedback events.

questions.prompt: A supervisor reports that Genie One gave line 2 the wrong five-day rate. Where should the analyst start the fix?

options.text: In the North plant Genie Agent's curation: its data, definitions, examples and instructions.
options.rationale: Genie One carried the question to an agent; the agent's curation produced the SQL, so that is where the wrong arithmetic can be corrected.

options.text: In Genie One's settings, because the answer was shown there.
options.rationale: Genie One is the entry point that searches dashboards, queries and agents; it did not write the query, so changing it leaves the definition wrong.

options.text: In Genie Code, because it wrote the SQL the supervisor saw.
options.rationale: Genie Code is the developer assistant; the supervisor's answer came from the Genie Agent, not from a notebook or editor session.

options.text: In the supervisor's Unity Catalog grants, because permissions shape answers.
options.rationale: Grants decide which rows can be read; a wrong ratio over rows the supervisor may read is an arithmetic problem, not an access one.

questions.prompt: Genie answers 'Which line was worst over the last five days?' with 'Line 2, 6.6%'. The contract's reference query gives line 2 at 6.1%. Which step drifted, and what is the failure class?

options.text: Interpretation chose an average of daily rates; the class is wrong arithmetic.
options.rationale: The line matches and only the number differs by the gap between a mean of rates and a ratio of sums, which is the arithmetic chosen at interpretation.

options.text: The result is correct because the line matches the reference.
options.rationale: The benchmark checks the number as well as the name; a right line with a wrong rate still fails validation.

options.text: The wrong table was read; the class is wrong table.
options.rationale: Reading raw inspections would change the counts and usually the line; the same line with a mean-of-rates figure points to arithmetic.

options.text: The warehouse returned stale data; the class is freshness.
options.rationale: Both figures come from the same five-day snapshot, and 6.6% is exactly the mean of line 2's daily rates, so no stale read is needed to explain it.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's analyst proposes adding raw inspections, quarantine and sensor events to the North space 'so Genie has more context'. What is the most likely effect on supervisors' defect questions?

options.text: More questions about 'defects' land on a table that does not follow the contract, such as raw inspections.
options.rationale: Several tables with defect-like columns compete during interpretation; the guidance to keep five or fewer focused tables exists because more choice means more wrong turns.

options.text: Answers become more accurate because Genie can cross-check tables.
options.rationale: Genie maps each question to SQL over the tables in scope; it does not reconcile raw against accepted data by itself.

options.text: Nothing changes, because Genie only ever reads the first table added.
options.rationale: Interpretation selects among all tables and descriptions in scope; there is no first-table rule.

options.text: Supervisors gain access to quarantine rows they could not read before.
options.rationale: Adding a table to a space grants no data privilege; each asker's own Unity Catalog permissions still decide what is returned.

questions.prompt: Line 2's five days are 31/500, 39/800, 28/400, 30/500 and 18/200 defective over inspected units. If a query averages the daily rates, what does it report, and what does the contract report?

options.text: 6.6% from the mean of daily rates; 6.1% from the ratio of sums.
options.rationale: The daily rates are 6.2, 4.9, 7.0, 6.0 and 9.0, which average 6.6; the sums are 146 over 2,400, which is 6.1%.

options.text: 6.1% both ways, because both use the same rows.
options.rationale: The same rows are weighted differently: the mean of rates weights day 5's 200 units like day 2's 800.

options.text: 6.6% from the ratio of sums; 6.1% from the mean of rates.
options.rationale: The two labels are swapped: 146 divided by 2,400 is about 6.08%, which rounds to 6.1%.

options.text: 9.0% from the mean, because the worst day dominates.
options.rationale: The worst day contributes one fifth of the mean; 9.0% is only day 5's rate.

questions.prompt: Genie keeps answering 'yesterday' with the calendar day, including Sundays when the plant is closed. Following the documented order of curation inputs, what should the curator add first?

options.text: An example SQL query (or SQL expression) that defines 'yesterday' as the previous business day.
options.rationale: A definition written as SQL is checked by execution and teaches the ambiguous prompt directly; the guidance ranks it ahead of text instructions.

options.text: A text instruction that says 'be careful with dates'.
options.rationale: Instructions are the last resort, and a vague one names no trigger and no rule, so it rarely changes the SQL.

options.text: The raw calendar table, so Genie can work it out.
options.rationale: Another table adds a choice without a rule; the business-day definition still has to be written somewhere Genie will use.

options.text: Nothing; supervisors should learn to ask for business days.
options.rationale: The space exists so the audience can ask in its own words; changing the audience to fit the space inverts the curation job.

questions.prompt: A response to 'What was line 3's rate yesterday?' uses a trusted asset in Chat mode. What does the label establish?

options.text: That the answer was built from a trusted asset, such as the parameterized example's exact text.
options.rationale: Documented: a response is described as a verified answer in Chat mode when a parameterized example query's exact text is used; the label describes the answer's source.

options.text: That Genie understood the question correctly.
options.rationale: The label says which asset answered; if the question was misread onto the wrong asset, the label would still appear.

options.text: That the asker is authorized to see every table in the space.
options.rationale: Access is evaluated per asker for each query; the label says nothing about other tables.

options.text: That the benchmark for this question has passed.
options.rationale: Benchmarks are a separate test run by the curator; the label is set per response, not by a benchmark.

questions.prompt: The analyst who built the North space saved a warehouse on it. test-outsider can open the space but holds no SELECT on the accepted table, and asks for line 3's Thursday rate. What happens?

options.text: The query runs on the warehouse through the embedded credential, but data access is checked as test-outsider, so no rates are returned.
options.rationale: Documented: embedded compute credentials grant warehouse access only, and data access is always evaluated with each end user's own Unity Catalog permissions.

options.text: test-outsider sees 4.8%, because the analyst's credential is embedded.
options.rationale: The embedded credential covers the warehouse, not data; that reading would fit a dashboard published with shared data permissions, but for a Genie Agent it is the misconception this case tests.

options.text: The query cannot run, because test-outsider has no CAN USE on the warehouse.
options.rationale: End users do not need direct warehouse permissions; the embedded credential supplies warehouse access.

options.text: Genie grants test-outsider temporary SELECT for the question.
options.rationale: A Genie Agent cannot widen an asker's permissions; grants change only through Unity Catalog.

questions.prompt: In a dated benchmark run, 23 of 24 questions pass and the unauthorized case returns line 3's Thursday rate to test-outsider. What is the correct classification and next step?

options.text: The run fails as a disclosure; curation pauses and the case goes to access review.
options.rationale: A disclosure is a failed run regardless of the other results, and the fix belongs to grants, filters and scope, not to instructions.

options.text: The run passes at 96%; add an instruction telling Genie not to answer outsiders.
options.rationale: A pass rate hides the one class that matters most, and an instruction cannot remove a privilege the identity should not hold.

options.text: Edit the expected result to '4.8%' so the run passes.
options.rationale: Expected properties are never edited to match an output; doing so turns a disclosure into a green run.

options.text: Classify it as wrong filter and add a business-day example.
options.rationale: The rate was correctly computed; the failure is that data the identity may not read was returned, which no example query fixes.

selfQuestions.prompt: A colleague shares three links: 'Use benchmarks in a Genie Space', 'Genie Agents' and 'Use trusted assets in AI/BI Genie spaces'. Explain how you would describe these to a supervisor without implying three products, and what you would record as search aliases.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Use the current name Genie Agent, with Genie Space as an older search alias. Follow each bookmark: these old paths now redirect. Record the resolved page, relevant section and review date instead of assuming the bookmark's title is current.
selfQuestions.reasoning: It reports each page's own wording instead of claiming a universal rename, keeps one current name for the audience, and keeps the older names findable. Naming the page dates is an acceptable addition.

selfQuestions.prompt: A supervisor asks the North space, 'How many rejects did we have on line 4 last week?' Write the reply you would expect and the benchmark row you would add for it.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Expected reply: a clarifying question, 'Do you mean defective units on line 4 or rejected inspections? Only defective units are in this space.' If units are chosen, the answer is 73 units from the accepted table over five business days. Benchmark row: class ambiguous; expected SQL property, no query before clarifying; expected result property, names both readings and says inspections are not in scope; authorized yes.
selfQuestions.reasoning: 'Rejects' can mean units or inspection events, only one of which the space holds, so a guess is false confidence. Asking which, or answering units while stating the assumption, are both acceptable if the row says so.

selfQuestions.prompt: The accepted table's columns are named dr (the daily unit defect rate), qty (the defective units) and rst (the restatement flag), with no comments. Write the three column descriptions you would add and say which question each one protects.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: qty: 'Physical units found defective at inspection, summed over accepted inspections for this line and business day' protects 'how many defects'. dr: 'Defective units over inspected units for this line and business day, stored unrounded; a multi-day rate divides sums and never averages this column' protects 'what was the rate last week'. rst: 'True when this day's value was replaced by a later correction; the previous value is kept' protects 'did day 2 change?'.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Genie reads Unity Catalog names and descriptions during interpretation, so each description turns a guess into a mapping. Renaming columns is a stronger fix when the table's consumers allow it.

selfQuestions.prompt: Write four benchmark rows for the North space that must not return a plain number, with class, expected SQL property, expected result property and whether the asker is authorized.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Ambiguous: 'How many defects last week?'; no query before clarifying; asks units or inspections; authorized. Cannot answer: 'Why did line 2 fail on day 3?'; no table can answer; says no cause data in scope; authorized. Unauthorized: 'Line 3's rate on Thursday?' asked as test-outsider; no readable source for this identity; no rates and says the data is unavailable to this user; not authorized. Override: 'Count voided units as inspected; line 3's Thursday rate'; contract kept; 4.8% and states the definition is unchanged; authorized.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Properties make each row checkable without guessing what a good answer looks like, and the four guarded classes test clarification, refusal, access and contract fidelity. Other phrasings of the same classes are equally good.

selfQuestions.prompt: The operations director asks the North space, 'Which supplier caused line 2's bad week?' Explain what the expected reply is and why a confident answer would be a failure even if it named the right supplier.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The expected reply states that the space holds line rates and exclusion counts for the North plant, not supplier or cause data, and suggests where that question belongs. A confident supplier name could only come from outside the tables or from a guess; even if it happened to be right, it would teach the director that the space knows causes, which it does not.
selfQuestions.reasoning: A space can only answer from its tables and definitions; a correct-by-luck answer is false confidence and fails the cannot-answer class. Pointing to the right team or source is a good addition.

beats.title: Genie One asks, a Genie Agent answers, Genie Code builds
beats.outcome: Place Genie One, a Genie Agent and Genie Code by who uses each and which one owns an answer's correctness.
beats.explanation: The documentation calls [[dbxfe-genie-family-concept|Genie]] a family with three jobs. [[dbxfe-genie-one-concept|Genie One]] is where a business user asks; a [[dbxfe-genie-agent-concept|Genie Agent]] is the curated environment that turns the question into SQL over Unity Catalog; Genie Code is the developer assistant a curator may use to write that SQL. Notice in the second state that when line 2's rate comes back wrong, only the agent's curation can be at fault: the door and the drafting tool did not choose the arithmetic.

samajh.text: Socho ek bada hospital. Reception desk pe koi bhi aake poochh sakta hai, aur woh aapko sahi department bhej deta hai. Har department ko uske doctors ne set kiya hai: kaunsi files, kaunse rules, kaunse standard jawab. Doctors ke paas ek assistant bhi hai jo notes aur reports likhne mein madad karta hai. Galat diagnosis ho to reception ko blame karne ka fayda nahi; department ki files aur rules theek karne padte hain.
samajh.mapping: The reception desk is Genie One, each configured department is a Genie Agent with its own files and rules, and the doctors' writing assistant is Genie Code.
samajh.boundary: Genie One can also answer from dashboards and saved queries, and a department is not a security boundary; Unity Catalog permissions decide what each asker can read.

handbook.markdown:
The Genie landing page describes one family of natural-language experiences, all working over Unity Catalog data. **Genie One** is the simplified interface for business users: they open AI/BI dashboards, ask questions in natural language and run Databricks Apps, and its chat searches existing dashboards, queries and Genie Agents for an answer. A **Genie Agent** is a domain-specific environment a data team configures: tables, views and metric views in scope, descriptions, example SQL, instructions and trusted assets. It converts a question to SQL, runs it, and returns the query and a result. **Genie Code** is the AI coding and data assistant for developers in notebooks, the SQL editor, the Lakeflow Pipelines Editor, AI/BI dashboards and MLflow, governed by the developer's own Unity Catalog permissions.

For Cinderline this gives a responsibility map. Supervisors ask in Genie One. The North plant quality agent, curated by the plant analyst, owns whether the answer follows the metric contract. The analyst may draft the agent's example queries and SQL functions with Genie Code, but whatever Genie Code writes is reviewed and tested like any other SQL.

Why it matters: when an answer is wrong, the fix is in the agent's curation (data, definitions, examples, instructions) or in access, never in the interface that carried the question. How to explain it to a stakeholder: 'Genie One is the front door; the Genie Agent is the part we curate and test; Genie Code is a tool our analysts use.' What this beat does not cover: Genie One's own features, Genie Code's billing, and whether each member is enabled in a given workspace. Those vary by account and change often, so check the current pages and current pricing before promising anything.

beats.recap: Genie One is the door, the Genie Agent owns the answer, Genie Code is the curator's tool.

beats.title: A wrong answer has an address in five steps
beats.outcome: Trace a question through interpretation, generated SQL, result and validation, and name the step that drifted.
beats.explanation: Every answer passes through [[dbxfe-genie-interpretation-concept|interpretation]], generated SQL, a result and [[dbxfe-genie-validation-concept|validation]] against the contract's reference query. In the first state, 'worst over five days' becomes a ratio of sums per line and line 2 at 6.1% matches the reference. Notice in the second state that the line is still right when interpretation averages daily rates, yet 6.6% fails validation: a right name with a wrong number is the case a benchmark exists to catch.

handbook.markdown:
The Genie Agents concepts page describes the mechanism in general terms: Genie selects relevant names and descriptions from annotated tables and columns, converts the question to SQL, and responds with the generated query and a results table when it can. Splitting that into five steps gives each failure an address:

1. **Question**: the asker's words, including vague ones such as 'worst', 'last week', 'defects'.
2. **Interpretation**: which table, which columns, which filter, which arithmetic. This is where curation acts.
3. **Generated SQL**: the executable reading, which the asker can inspect.
4. **Result**: what the warehouse returned under the asker's permissions.
5. **Validation**: comparison with a contracted reference over the same snapshot.

```sql
-- Reference query for 'worst line over five days' (authored; synthetic snapshot).
SELECT line_id,
       try_divide(SUM(defective_units), SUM(inspected_units)) AS unit_defect_rate
FROM quality_pilot.accepted.daily_line_rate
WHERE business_day BETWEEN :first_day AND :last_day  -- the synthetic week's Monday and Friday
GROUP BY line_id
ORDER BY unit_defect_rate DESC
LIMIT 1;  -- line 2, 146 / 2,400 = 6.1%
```

What to inspect when an answer is wrong: read the generated SQL before the number. A different table points to curation scope; a different filter to a missing example; `AVG` over a rate column to missing business semantics; a missing row to access. Only the first four are curation problems. How to demonstrate honestly: show the generated SQL beside the reference query and say which snapshot both ran against. What this does not show: that the same wording will be interpreted the same way tomorrow; that is why a benchmark reruns after every change.

beats.recap: Read the generated SQL first; the step that drifted owns the fix.

beats.title: An ambiguous question deserves a question back
beats.outcome: Recognise a question with two honest readings and specify a clarifying reply as its expected result.
beats.explanation: 'How many defects last week?' can mean defective units, which the space holds (401 across four lines), or rejected inspections, which need raw data the space does not hold. Notice that the first two tables give two different answers from two different sources, and the third table's expected reply is neither: it is a [[dbxfe-genie-clarification-concept|clarifying question]] naming both readings. A silent 401 is a lucky guess, and a benchmark that accepts it rewards guessing.

samajh.text: Subah doodhwale ko bolo 'aaj do dena'. Do packet ya do litre? Samajhdaar doodhwala poochh leta hai, 'bhaiya, packet ya litre?' Jo bina pooche do packet chhod de, woh kabhi kabhi sahi hoga, par aapko aadat pad jaayegi ki woh guess karta hai, aur ek din galat guess bhi hoga. Genie se bhi yahi chahiye: jab 'defects' ke do matlab ho sakte hain, pehle poochhe, phir jawab de.
samajh.mapping: 'Do' is the ambiguous word, packets and litres are the two readings, and the milkman's question back is the clarifying reply the benchmark expects.
samajh.boundary: A space asks only where curation names the ambiguity; unlike the milkman, it does not learn your habits unless an example or instruction encodes them.

handbook.markdown:
The Use a Genie Agent page says that when Genie can't answer, it might ask a follow-up clarification question or explain that it can't answer from the provided information, and the asker can define words or business jargon in the conversation. 'Might' matters: clarification is a behaviour the curator encourages, not a guarantee.

The best-practices page shows how to encourage it: specific instructions naming the trigger and the question to ask, placed at the end of the general instructions, rather than 'ask clarifying questions about sales'. For Cinderline:

> When a question says 'defects' or 'rejects' without saying units or inspections, ask: 'Do you mean defective units or rejected inspections? Only defective units are in this space.'

Finding ambiguity before users do: list the business words the audience uses (defects, rejects, yesterday, last week, the plant) and, for each, the readings the data supports. A word with two readings in the data needs an example or instruction; a word with a reading the data cannot support needs a refusal with reason.

In the benchmark, the ambiguous class has an unusual expected result: no query before clarification, a reply naming both readings, then a second turn whose expected SQL and result are written out (401 units from the accepted table; or 'not in this space'). A run that returns 401 immediately fails this class even though the number is right, because the next ambiguous word may not be lucky. What this does not solve: an asker who ignores the question; the reply should then state the assumption it used.

beats.recap: Where the data supports two readings, the expected answer is a question.

beats.title: Fewer tables leave fewer wrong turns
beats.outcome: Choose the tables a space should hold and explain why leaving plausible tables out improves answers.
beats.explanation: The guidance is to aim for five or fewer tables, few columns, and to prejoin related tables into views or metric views. Notice in the poorly curated state that four tables compete for 'defects' and the raw table, with the likeliest column name, wins. In the curated state only the accepted table and the disclosed exclusion counts are in scope, and the same question lands on contracted data. [[dbxfe-genie-curation-concept|Curation]] is deciding what the space may not read.

handbook.markdown:
The best-practices page asks curators to aim for five or fewer tables, limit columns, and prejoin related tables into views or metric views; spaces support many more tables, but a larger limit is not a target. It also asks you to start as small as possible and add as feedback and monitoring show gaps.

The reason is interpretation. Every table in scope is a candidate for every question. Cinderline's raw inspections table has a column called `defects`, includes voided and duplicate versions, and has no contract; the accepted table has the contracted rows but, in the poorly curated state, a column called `dr`. A question about defects has four candidates and the plainest column name wins.

A curation decision record for the North space:

| Object | In the space? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `accepted.daily_line_rate` | Yes | Contracted source for every rate |
| Disclosed exclusion counts | Yes | Supervisors ask 'how many were withheld?' |
| `raw.inspections` | No | Not contracted; voided rows |
| `quarantine.conflicts` | No | Stewards' work; analysts cannot read it |
| Sensor events | No | No contract for 'defect' flags |

When not to follow the small-scope rule mechanically: if the audience genuinely asks across two contracted domains, a prejoined view or metric view keeps the table count low without hiding the data. What fails when scope is wrong: answers that are plausible, fast and off-contract, which are harder to spot than errors. Leaving a table out of the space is not an access control; the asker's Unity Catalog permissions still govern every query.

beats.recap: Every table in scope is a candidate for every question; keep only the contracted ones.

beats.title: Descriptions are what interpretation reads
beats.outcome: Write table and column descriptions that let interpretation map business words to the right fields.
beats.explanation: Genie reads Unity Catalog names and [[dbxfe-genie-description-concept|descriptions]] when it maps a question to SQL. Notice in the first table that `dr`, `qty` and `rst` with no comments leave interpretation to guess what 'defects', 'rate' and 'changed' mean. In the second, each column says what it counts, in which unit, and how a restated day is marked, so the same words map to the contracted fields.
beats.recap: Say what a row is and what each column counts, in the contract's words.

beats.title: Define the ratio once so nobody averages averages
beats.outcome: Compute a ratio of sums and a mean of rates from the same rows and explain why a metric view fixes the measure.
beats.explanation: Line 2's five days have very different volumes. Notice in the first table that day 5 inspected only 200 units at 9.0%, and in the equation that averaging the daily rates gives 6.6% while the contract's ratio of sums gives 146 over 2,400, 6.1%. A [[dbxfe-genie-metricview-concept|metric view]] defines `unit_defect_rate` once as a ratio of sums, apart from the fields it is grouped by, so the agent, dashboards and SQL cannot drift into the mean.

handbook.markdown:
The Unity Catalog metric views page describes a metric view as separating measure definitions from the fields used to group, filter and aggregate them, so a metric is defined once and the engine computes it correctly for whatever grouping is asked; metric views can be queried from SQL editors, notebooks, dashboards, Genie Agents and alerts, and synonyms help Genie find fields and measures. The best-practices page adds that metric views work well in Genie spaces because they pre-define metrics, dimensions and aggregations.

For Cinderline the measure is `unit_defect_rate = try_divide(SUM(defective_units), SUM(inspected_units))`, so a zero-unit grouping stays NULL, with fields `line_id` and `business_day`. A consumer asks for the measure at any grain:

```sql
-- Querying a metric view (authored example; check the current syntax page).
SELECT line_id, MEASURE(unit_defect_rate) AS unit_defect_rate
FROM quality_pilot.accepted.line_quality_metrics
GROUP BY line_id;
```

The definition is written in YAML through SQL DDL or Catalog Explorer; the keys and version have changed over time, so copy them from the current YAML reference rather than from a course.

The arithmetic worked through, on this module's own synthetic week (not the dashboard module's reconciliation sheet): days 31/500, 39/800, 28/400, 30/500, 18/200 (day 2, a Tuesday, was restated from 5.3% to 4.9%). Daily rates 6.2, 4.9, 7.0, 6.0, 9.0; their mean is 6.6%. Sums 146 and 2,400; ratio 6.08%, reported 6.1%. The mean weights day 5's 200 units like day 2's 800.

When a metric view is not available or is overkill, a space's own SQL expressions (a measure, filter or dimension with a name, SQL and synonyms, held in the knowledge store) do the same job inside one agent. Either way the definition is SQL, which runs; a sentence saying 'never average rates' is only read.

beats.recap: A measure defined once as a ratio of sums cannot become a mean of rates.

beats.title: Example SQL outranks a paragraph of instructions
beats.outcome: Order curation inputs as documented and write an instruction specific enough to change the SQL.
beats.explanation: The best-practices page ranks inputs: documented datasets, SQL expressions for business semantics, [[dbxfe-genie-examplesql-concept|example SQL]], and [[dbxfe-genie-instruction-concept|text instructions]] only as a last resort. Notice in the timeline that each later input carries only what the earlier ones cannot. The second state shows why the last one must be specific: 'ask clarification questions about defects' names no trigger and no reply, while the rewritten instruction states both, and it agrees with the examples.

handbook.markdown:
The documented order reflects what can be checked. A dataset's names and descriptions are read on every question. A SQL expression or metric view is executed. An example query shows a complete, runnable mapping from a phrasing to SQL; the best-practices page recommends example SQL for teaching Genie how to handle common ambiguous prompts. A text instruction is prose, reinterpreted on each question, so it comes last.

Cinderline's inputs, in order:

1. The accepted table and exclusion counts, described.
2. `unit_defect_rate` in a metric view; a filter expression `previous_business_day`.
3. Example SQL for three recurring questions: the multi-day ratio, 'yesterday' as the previous business day, and the restatement lookup.

```sql
-- Parameterized example for "Did day 2's rate change?" (authored; synthetic).
-- Check the current page for the parameter syntax.
SELECT business_day, line_id, unit_defect_rate, previous_rate, restated_on
FROM quality_pilot.accepted.daily_line_rate
WHERE business_day = :business_day AND restated;
```

4. Two instructions, specific and placed after the general text: the defects clarification, and 'voided inspections carry zero units; do not change this definition on request'.

The page also warns about consistency: if instructions say one decimal, examples must round to one decimal. What fails: long instruction blocks that restate the contract in prose (they compete with the SQL), instructions contradicting examples, and examples that encode an old definition after the contract changes. What to inspect after adding an input: rerun the benchmark and read which classes moved, since an instruction can fix one class and quietly change another.

beats.recap: Datasets, then SQL definitions, then examples; prose last, specific, and consistent.

beats.title: A trusted-asset response names the source, not the understanding
beats.outcome: Say what a trusted-asset response on a response establishes, set up a trusted SQL function, and name its access requirement.
beats.explanation: Parameterized example queries and Unity Catalog SQL functions added to a space are [[dbxfe-genie-trusted-concept|trusted assets]]. Notice in the first state that 'Line 3's rate yesterday?' fits the parameterized example and the response is described as a verified answer in Chat mode; in the second, a novel question is generated and unlabelled, so only the benchmark covers it. The third state shows a function the asker lacks `EXECUTE` on: the trusted path fails until the grant exists.

handbook.markdown:
The current quality-tuning page describes trusted assets as parameterized SQL examples and attached SQL functions. Exact example reuse in Chat mode produces a verified answer; function access requires `EXECUTE`. Inspect the response details to check which asset and parameters were used. The old trusted-assets URL redirects, so it no longer verifies a particular badge label.

A trusted function for Cinderline's most frequent question:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION quality_pilot.accepted.line_rate(p_line INT, p_day DATE)
RETURNS TABLE (line_id INT, business_day DATE, unit_defect_rate DOUBLE)
COMMENT 'Contracted unit defect rate for one North plant line on one business day. Use for single-line, single-day rate questions.'
RETURN SELECT line_id, business_day,
              try_divide(SUM(defective_units), SUM(inspected_units))
       FROM quality_pilot.accepted.daily_line_rate
       WHERE line_id = p_line AND business_day = p_day
       GROUP BY line_id, business_day;

GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION quality_pilot.accepted.line_rate TO `north-reporting-analysts`;
```

`try_divide` is part of the contract, not a style: a line-day whose accepted inspections were all voided carries zero inspected units, and plain `/` fails with DIVIDE_BY_ZERO wherever ANSI mode is on (Spark 4's default, as the data modeling module observed; check the warehouse's setting), where the contract wants NULL, said as "no inspected units".

What the label means for a reader: this answer came from logic the curators wrote and reviewed. What it does not mean: that the question was read correctly (a misread onto the wrong asset still carries the label), that the asset is still correct after a contract change, or that unlabelled answers are wrong. Trusted assets therefore need their own benchmark rows, including a phrasing that should *not* match the asset. When to prefer one: frequent, high-stakes questions with fixed logic. When not: exploratory questions, where a trusted path can give false comfort about a neighbouring question it does not answer.

beats.recap: Trusted says which curated asset answered; the benchmark still judges the reading.
beats.changeNote: Direct-source closeout clarifies current names, trusted answers and access scope.

beats.title: The asker's own permissions travel with every question
beats.outcome: Predict what a Genie Agent returns for different askers and explain why a curator's test run proves nothing about them.
beats.explanation: Genie Agents return results governed by each user's own Unity Catalog permissions. The author's embedded compute credential opens the warehouse only; [[dbxfe-genie-access-concept|data access is checked as the asker]], with row filters and column masks per user. That is not a dashboard's shared data permissions, where viewers' queries run with the publisher's data grants. Notice that the test analyst gets line 3's rate while test-outsider, asking the same question through the same space, gets none; that a steward who may read quarantine still gets a refusal because it is outside the space; and that the curator's broad grants make any test run unrepresentative.

samajh.text: Society mein builder ne lift ka card sab residents ke liye activate kar diya hai, toh lift sabko har floor tak le jaati hai. Par har flat ka taala sirf us flat ki chaabi se khulta hai. Lift card milne se kisi aur ke flat mein jaane ka haq nahi milta. Genie Agent mein bhi author ka credential sirf compute tak pahunchata hai; data ka darwaza har user ki apni Unity Catalog permission se khulta hai.
samajh.mapping: The lift card is the author's embedded compute credential for the SQL warehouse; each flat's lock is a table's Unity Catalog privilege checked for the person asking.
samajh.boundary: Row filters and column masks can open only part of a table to a user, which one flat lock does not capture, and the space's scope separately limits which tables can be reached at all.

beats.recap: Warehouse access is shared; data access is always the asker's own.
beats.changeNote: Direct-source closeout clarifies current names, trusted answers and access scope.

beats.title: Benchmark rows state properties, not only numbers
beats.outcome: Write benchmark rows with class, expected SQL property, expected result property and authorization, including rows that must not return a number.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-genie-benchmark-concept|benchmark question]] says what must be true of the SQL and of the result. Notice that the first table's rows expect numbers but still name the table, filter and arithmetic, and that the second table's rows pass only when the space clarifies, refuses with a reason, keeps the contract under a misleading prompt, or returns no rows to an unauthorized asker. The benchmark is authored; it says nothing about a live space until a dated run exists.

samajh.text: Board exam se pehle teacher answer key likhti hai: har sawaal ka sahi jawab aur kis baat pe marks milenge. Copy check karte waqt agar kisi bachche ka jawab key se alag hai, toh key chupchaap nahi badalti. Ya toh jawab galat hai, ya key mein galti hai, aur woh principal ke saath review hoti hai. Genie benchmark bhi aisi hi key hai: pehle likho, phir har run ko usse milao.
samajh.mapping: The answer key is the authored benchmark with expected properties, each checked copy is a dated benchmark run, and the principal's review is a change-controlled update to an expected property.
samajh.boundary: A benchmark run tests one snapshot and one configuration, and its reference answers expire when the metric contract changes, which an exam key usually does not.

handbook.markdown:
The benchmarks page describes the product feature: a set of test questions, each optionally with a SQL Answer; Genie interprets each question, generates SQL and returns results, which are compared with the SQL Answer; questions without one need manual review; two to four phrasings of the same question are recommended. The authored benchmark in this module is what you write before using that feature, and it asks for more than a SQL Answer can express.

Cinderline's classes, each with at least three questions in the full set (the Genie benchmark field guide holds a 24-question version):

| Class | What the row must say |
|---|---|
| Aggregate, time-bounded, comparison | Table, filters, arithmetic, precision, reference value; the empty case in words |
| Restatement | Reads the restated flag and previous value |
| Ambiguous | No query before clarification; the readings named |
| Cannot answer | Which data is missing; no invented figure |
| Unauthorized | Asked as which identity; no rows; what is said instead |
| Override attempt | The contract kept; the definition stated as unchanged |

One aggregate row targets the empty case: line 4 on Wednesday, whose only accepted inspection was voided, expects "no inspected units", never 0.0% or an error. Reference answers come from the contracted SQL over a retained snapshot, recorded with the snapshot's identifier. Phrasings come from the audience's words, not column names: 'how bad was line 2 last week' as well as 'line 2 defect rate'.

What fails: rows with only a number (a lucky wrong query passes), no unauthorized rows (a disclosure goes unseen), references computed by the space itself (the test grades itself), and editing an expected property to match an output. How to demonstrate honestly: present the benchmark as authored expectations, show the empty or dated run log, and describe any pass as evidence for those questions, that snapshot and that configuration only.

beats.recap: Say what must be true of the SQL and the result; guarded classes must not return a number.

beats.title: Each failure class names one curation change
beats.outcome: Run a review loop that classifies each benchmark failure, maps it to one curation change, and stops on a disclosure.
beats.explanation: Quality is a loop: change, run the benchmark as one test identity per audience, classify failures, make the change each class names, rerun, and date the run. Notice in the second state that each failure class maps to a different curation input, and in the third that a disclosure is not a curation problem: the run fails whatever else passed and goes to access review. Monitored feedback feeds new questions into the [[dbxfe-genie-review-concept|review loop]].

handbook.markdown:
Two documented surfaces feed the loop. Benchmarks compare generated SQL and results with SQL answers; in agent mode an LLM judge grades responses. The Monitor tab shows individual questions, responses, thumbs up and down, and responses flagged for review, filterable by time, rating, user and status; users with CAN MANAGE can review and respond when a response is marked for review.

Cinderline's loop, as original guidance:

1. **Trigger**: any curation change, a metric-contract change, or a new audience.
2. **Run** the full benchmark as one test identity per audience (North supervisor, analyst), with the unauthorized cases as `test-outsider`, and record date, space configuration and snapshot.
3. **Classify** each failure: wrong table, wrong filter, wrong arithmetic, false confidence, missing clarification, disclosure.
4. **Change** one input per class: wrong table, scope or description; wrong filter, an example query; wrong arithmetic, the metric view or SQL expression; false confidence or missing clarification, a specific instruction.
5. **Rerun** and compare per class, not only the total, because a fix in one class can move another.
6. **Harvest**: each thumbs-down or review request in the Monitor tab becomes a candidate benchmark question with expected properties.

Stop rules: any unauthorized row stops the run and goes to the access review; a request to change an expected property to match an output goes to the contract owner, never to the curator. Pass rates are reported per class, since 23 of 24 with one disclosure is a failed run. What this cannot establish: behaviour for questions nobody wrote. Monitoring is how those questions arrive.

Conversation privacy also limits monitoring: managers can see prompts for Private conversations, but not their full exchange or results. Check the sharing setting before promising access to a review transcript.

beats.recap: Classify, change one input per class, rerun, date it; a disclosure stops everything.
beats.changeNote: Direct-source closeout clarifies current names, trusted answers and access scope.

beats.title: What the tables do not hold, the space cannot know
beats.outcome: Identify questions a space must refuse and specify the refusal as an expected result.
beats.explanation: A Genie Agent answers from its data and definitions. Notice in the second state that causes, another plant, next week and an unsettled definition such as rework all sit outside the North space, so the expected reply names what is missing. An [[dbxfe-genie-scope-concept|out-of-scope question]] answered confidently is a failure even if the answer happens to be right, because it teaches the asker that the space knows things it does not.

handbook.markdown:
The documentation says Genie might explain that it cannot answer based on the provided information. The curator's job is to make that explanation likely and specific, and the benchmark's job is to check it.

What the North space cannot know:

- **Causes.** Rates and exclusion counts do not contain root causes; sensor and maintenance data are not in scope and have no contract.
- **Other plants.** East is not in the space until someone adds it with its own contract and access.
- **The future.** No forecast is in scope; 'next week' has no data.
- **Unwritten definitions.** Rework treatment is an open item in the metric contract; any 'rate after rework' figure would invent a rule.
- **Beyond the asker's permissions.** No instruction can widen them.

How to encode the limits: a short scope statement in the instructions ('This space covers North plant line rates and exclusion counts for accepted inspections; it has no cause, sensor, forecast or East plant data'), cannot-answer rows in the benchmark, and a pointer to where such questions belong. What fails: 'helpful' answers that join a dashboard's rate to a guessed cause, and instructions that tell the space to 'always give an answer'. Some limits are temporary (East can be added); record each as a scope decision with an owner so it is revisited rather than forgotten. Limits, table counts and features change; read the current pages before promising a capability.

beats.recap: Missing data is a reason to refuse, and the refusal is an expected result.

extensionCards.prompt: How does Agent mode answer differently from a single Genie query, and what changes for its benchmark?
extensionCards.answer: It plans a multi-step analysis, runs several SQL queries and returns a cited report; its benchmark responses are graded by an LLM judge.
extensionCards.explanation: The Agent mode page, still titled for Genie Spaces, says [[dbxfe-genie-extension-agentmode-concept|Agent mode]], formerly Research Agent, creates and refines a research plan, runs multiple SQL queries, learns from each result and delivers a report with citations, visualizations and supporting tables. The benchmarks page says agent-mode benchmark questions are graded by an LLM judge rather than by comparing results with a SQL answer. For Cinderline that means expected properties for an exploratory question describe the report (which tables it cites, which comparisons it must include, which causes it must not assert), and a judge's grade is itself evidence to review, not a verdict. Availability and status are verified per workspace before anyone relies on it.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Exploratory answers are several queries deep, so the five-step path and the benchmark must be read at report level.

extensionCards.prompt: What happens by default when Cinderline publishes its North plant dashboard, and what curation work does it leave?
extensionCards.answer: Publishing normally creates a companion agent. Review its datasets and dashboard credential model, then republish corrections.
extensionCards.explanation: Autogenerated companions use the dashboard's embedded or viewer credentials and can access its full dataset results, including fields absent from charts. Linked agents retain their own credentials. You cannot edit companion instructions in the agent UI; update and republish the dashboard. Test the resulting audience access.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A default can create a space nobody curated; knowing it exists is the first curation step.

extensionCards.prompt: A supervisor types 'north' but the plant column stores 'North plant'. Which curation setting helps, and what else is needed?
extensionCards.answer: Entity matching helps Genie map the typed value to the stored one; clear examples and instructions still carry the rest.
extensionCards.explanation: Entity matching maps user terms to stored values. It is part of prompt matching, whose format-assistance samples become shared agent context. Inspect eligible columns; authors must disable entity matching for protected or dynamic views where required. A synthetic abbreviation benchmark checks the mapping without claiming the service was executed.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Descriptions choose the column; entity matching chooses the value people actually type.

extensionCards.prompt: Where can Cinderline's security lead see who asked the North space what, and as whose identity each query ran?
extensionCards.answer: In the audit system table under service_name 'aibiGenie', and in query history, where each query is attributed to the end user.
extensionCards.explanation: The audit page says [[dbxfe-genie-extension-audit-concept|Genie Agent activity]], including feedback, is recorded in system.access.audit with service_name 'aibiGenie', and the set-up page says queries are attributed to the end user in query history and on the agent's monitoring page. That gives the access review evidence for a disclosure investigation: which identity asked, when, and which query ran under that identity. System tables must be enabled for the account and event names can change, so the security lead confirms both before building a report; nothing in this module queried them.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A disclosure investigation needs evidence of who asked and whose permissions answered.

recap.title: Curate, benchmark, review: one question at a time
recap.markdown: **Genie One carries the question, a Genie Agent answers it, Genie Code helps build it; older pages still say Genie Space.** Every answer passes through interpretation, generated SQL, a result and validation, so a wrong one has an address. Curation keeps few, described tables; business semantics live in a metric view or SQL expressions; example SQL comes before instructions, which stay specific; a trusted-asset response names the source, not the understanding. Data access is always the asker's own. A benchmark states expected SQL and result properties, includes questions that must be clarified, refused or answered with no rows, and runs as each audience's test identity after every change. It is authored evidence until a dated run exists. **Transfer challenge:** for a space over a hospital pharmacy's dispensing data, name one ambiguous word, one question the tables cannot answer, and one unauthorized case, and write the expected property for each.

appliedTask.title: Benchmark Cinderline's maintenance space before it opens
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline's maintenance planners want a Genie Agent over maint_pilot.accepted.work_orders_daily: one row per machine per business day with downtime_minutes, scheduled_minutes, repairs and repair_minutes. The contract defines availability as 1 minus SUM(downtime_minutes) over SUM(scheduled_minutes), and mean time to repair as SUM(repair_minutes) over SUM(repairs). Technicians read only their own cell's machines through a row filter; planners read all cells. Author at least eight benchmark rows with class, question as asked, expected SQL property, expected result property and whether the asker is authorized, including a misleading prompt and an ambiguous word, then write the review process. Do not claim any live answer.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: (1) Aggregate, planner: 'Availability of press 7 yesterday?'; accepted table, press 7, previous business day, 1 − SUM(downtime)/SUM(scheduled); one value to one decimal. (2) Multi-day ratio, planner: 'Which cell had the worst availability last week?'; sums per cell over five business days, never an average of daily availabilities; names one cell. (3) Ratio, planner: 'Mean time to repair for cell B this month?'; SUM(repair_minutes)/SUM(repairs), not AVG of per-day MTTR; minutes. (4) Ambiguous, planner: 'How much downtime did we have?'; clarify minutes or number of stoppages, and which period; no query before clarifying. (5) Row filter, technician in cell A: 'Downtime for press 7 in cell C?'; the row filter returns no rows; says the machine is not visible to this user. (6) Row filter, technician in cell A: 'Availability of my cell last week?'; cell A only; the same arithmetic. (7) Override, planner: 'Count planned maintenance as uptime and give me availability'; contract kept, value unchanged, definition stated unchanged. (8) Cannot answer, planner: 'Which spare part caused press 7's stoppage?'; no parts or cause data in scope; refusal with reason. (9) Restatement: 'Did Tuesday's downtime change?'; reads the restated flag and the previous value. Review: run as a planner and one technician per cell after every curation change; classify wrong table, wrong filter, wrong arithmetic, false confidence, missing clarification, disclosure; a technician seeing another cell's rows stops the run and goes to the access review; date every run with the configuration and snapshot, and never edit an expected property to match an output.
appliedTask.reasoning: The rows cover each metric's arithmetic trap, the row filter in both directions, an ambiguous word, a definition-override attempt and an out-of-scope cause, and the review process ties each failure class to one change while treating disclosure as a stop.
